scenarioData.doorDesc: Step-by-step scripts to speak through the door without opening it.
scenarioData.doorStep1Script: Who is it? What do you want?
scenarioData.doorStep1Explanation: Never open the door. Speak through it.
scenarioData.doorStep2Script: Please slide your identification under the door or hold it up to the window.
scenarioData.doorStep2Explanation: You have the right to verify who they are.
scenarioData.doorStep3Script: Do you have a warrant signed by a judge? Please slide it under the door.
scenarioData.doorStep3Explanation: ICE needs a judicial warrant (signed by a judge) to enter. An administrative warrant is NOT enough.
scenarioData.doorStep4Script: I do not consent to you entering my home. I am exercising my right to remain silent and want to speak to a lawyer.
scenarioData.doorStep4Explanation: 5th Amendment protects your right to remain silent.
scenarioData.doorStep5Script: Start recording audio/video through a window if safe to do so.
scenarioData.doorStep5Explanation: You have the right to document law enforcement at your door.
scenarioData.doorOverview: ICE cannot enter your home without a judicial warrant signed by a judge. You have constitutional rights that protect you.
scenarioData.doorKeyPoint2: ✓ Ask to see the warrant through the door/window
scenarioData.doorKeyPoint3: ✓ Check if the warrant is signed by a judge (judicial) vs. an ICE officer (administrative)
scenarioData.doorKeyPoint4: ✓ Administrative warrants do NOT give ICE permission to enter your home
scenarioData.doorKeyPoint5: ✓ You have the right to remain silent
scenarioData.doorKeyPoint6: ✓ You can refuse to answer questions
scenarioData.doorWarrantJudicialDesc: Allows ICE to enter your home
scenarioData.doorWarrantAdminDesc: Does NOT allow entry to your home
scenarioData.doorDecision3OptionA: A judicial warrant — signed by a judge
scenarioData.doorBranch3aScript: I need a moment to read this warrant.
scenarioData.doorBranch3aExplanation: A valid judicial warrant must name your specific address and carry a judge's signature and date — not an ICE officer's. Read it carefully through the door or window. Confirm the address matches before complying.
scenarioData.doorBranch3bScript: This is not a judicial warrant. I am not required to open this door. Please leave.
scenarioData.doorBranch3bExplanation: I-200 (Warrant for Arrest of Alien) and I-205 (Warrant of Removal) are signed by ICE officers, not judges. They do NOT authorize entry into your home. You are within your rights to keep the door closed.
scenarioData.doorBranch3cScript: Without a judicial warrant signed by a judge, I will not open this door. Please leave.
scenarioData.doorBranch3cExplanation: ICE cannot legally enter without a valid judicial warrant. Keeping the door closed is your constitutional right. Remain calm and do not open the door.
scenarioData.doorBranch1aScript: Quietly assign roles: one person speaks, one records, one calls your attorney. Move children away from doors and windows.
scenarioData.doorBranch1aExplanation: Divide responsibilities silently before responding. A designated caller can contact your attorney or trusted contact while you manage the door. Keep children calm and away from sight lines of any windows or doors.
scenarioData.doorBranch1bScript: Begin recording audio now if safe to do so. Continue to step 2.
scenarioData.doorBranch1bExplanation: Start documenting immediately. You have full rights regardless of whether others are home. Note the time and proceed through the steps.
scenarioData.doorDecision4OptionA: They entered without consent or a valid judicial warrant
scenarioData.doorDecision4OptionB: They are still at the door and have not entered
scenarioData.doorBranch4aScript: I do not consent to your presence in my home. I am not resisting but I do not consent. I want to speak to a lawyer immediately.
scenarioData.doorBranch4aExplanation: Do not physically resist — it escalates danger and adds charges. Verbally assert non-consent clearly for any witnesses or recording. Note badge numbers, names, what they search, and what they take. Call your attorney the moment they leave.
scenarioData.doorBranch4bScript: Continue to step 5 — document the encounter from a safe location inside your home.
scenarioData.doorBranch4bExplanation: Your rights assertion is working. Continue documenting from behind a closed door. Note everything you observe through windows.
scenarioData.doorStep6Script: I will not sign any documents without my lawyer present.
scenarioData.doorStep6Explanation: Any document they present — including I-407 (voluntary departure), I-200 (arrest warrant), or any consent form — could permanently waive your legal rights and right to appeal. Never sign without an attorney reviewing it first.
scenarioData.streetDesc: Are you free to leave? How to exercise silence in public.
scenarioData.streetStep1Action: ASK IF YOU ARE FREE TO LEAVE
scenarioData.streetStep1Explanation: This is the most important question. If they say yes, calmly walk away.
scenarioData.streetStep2Script: I am exercising my right to remain silent. I do not wish to answer any questions.
scenarioData.streetStep2Explanation: You have the 5th Amendment right to remain silent.
scenarioData.streetStep3Script: I do not consent to any searches.
scenarioData.streetStep4Script: I want to speak to a lawyer.
scenarioData.streetStep4Explanation: You have the right to legal representation.
scenarioData.streetStep5Script: Keep your hands visible. Do not run. Remain calm and respectful.
scenarioData.streetStep5Explanation: De-escalation is key to your safety.
scenarioData.streetOverview: In public spaces, ICE may approach you. You have the right to remain silent and the right to ask if you are free to leave. Do not run, lie, or show false documents.
scenarioData.streetKeyPoint1: ✓ Always ask "Am I free to leave?"
scenarioData.streetKeyPoint2: ✓ You have the right to remain silent
scenarioData.streetKeyPoint3: ✓ You do not have to answer questions about your immigration status
scenarioData.streetKeyPoint4: ✓ Do not run or physically resist
scenarioData.streetKeyPoint5: ✓ Do not lie or provide false documents
scenarioData.streetKeyPoint6: ✓ Stay calm and keep hands visible
scenarioData.streetWarrantJudicialDesc: Ask if you are free to leave. Exercise your right to silence. Request a lawyer.
scenarioData.streetWarrantAdminDesc: Do not run. Do not lie. Do not show false documents. Do not physically resist.
scenarioData.streetBranch1aScript: Walk away calmly. Keep your hands visible. Do not run.
scenarioData.streetBranch1aExplanation: Leave immediately but calmly. Walking away is your right. Do not run — it can escalate the situation and may be used against you.
scenarioData.streetBranch1bScript: What is the legal basis for my detention? I am exercising my right to remain silent and want to speak to a lawyer.
scenarioData.streetBranch1bExplanation: If detained, they must have reasonable suspicion. Asking the legal basis puts it on record. Continue to the remaining steps — stay silent and repeat your lawyer request.
scenarioData.streetBranch1cScript: I am taking your non-answer as consent to leave. I am going now.
scenarioData.streetBranch1cExplanation: A non-answer or evasion can be treated as implicit permission to leave. Say this clearly and walk away calmly. Do not run.
scenarioData.streetBranch3aScript: I do not consent to this search. I am not resisting, but I am not consenting.
scenarioData.streetBranch3aExplanation: Say this clearly for the record. Do not physically resist — it escalates danger and adds charges. Your verbal refusal is legally significant and can be used to challenge the search in court. Note what they search and what they take.
scenarioData.streetBranch3bScript: Continue to step 4 — request a lawyer and maintain your right to silence.
scenarioData.streetBranch3bExplanation: Your refusal worked. Stay calm, keep hands visible. Do not assume the encounter is over.
scenarioData.streetBranch2aScript: I need an interpreter. I do not speak English well enough to understand my rights.
scenarioData.streetBranch2aExplanation: You have the right to an interpreter in legal proceedings. Do not attempt to communicate through limited language — misunderstandings can be used against you. Request an interpreter clearly and repeat the request if it is denied.
scenarioData.streetBranch2bScript: Continue asserting your right to silence.
scenarioData.streetBranch2bExplanation: Continue through the steps. Your silence is your strongest protection.
scenarioData.streetBranch4aScript: I am exercising my right to remain silent. I want to speak to a lawyer. I am a citizen of [your country] and I request consular notification.
scenarioData.streetBranch4aExplanation: Under the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations, non-citizens detained by law enforcement have the right to consular notification — the right to have their country's consulate informed and to receive consular assistance. State your country clearly and repeat this request if it is denied.
scenarioData.streetBranch4bScript: I am exercising my right to remain silent. I want to speak to a lawyer.
scenarioData.streetBranch4bExplanation: As a US citizen you have full constitutional protections including the right to silence and the right to an attorney. Repeat these requests clearly and calmly.
scenarioData.streetBranch5aScript: Can someone please witness this interaction and note the officer's badge number?
scenarioData.streetBranch5aExplanation: Loudly and calmly calling for witnesses deters misconduct and creates additional documentation. You are not directing anyone to interfere — only to observe. Witnesses can provide statements to your attorney later.
scenarioData.streetBranch5bScript: State your name and location aloud if you are recording. My name is [name] and I am at [location].
scenarioData.streetBranch5bExplanation: If no witnesses are present, verbal documentation for any recording device is important. State identifying details clearly. Note badge numbers, agency markings, and time.
scenarioData.streetStep6Script: I will not sign any documents without my lawyer present.
scenarioData.streetStep6Explanation: Officers may present consent-to-search forms, voluntary departure paperwork, or other documents during or after a stop. Do not sign anything. Any signature could waive legal rights you don't realize you're giving up. Wait for your attorney.
scenarioData.vehicleDesc: Rights during ICE traffic stops. Warrant vs consent.
scenarioData.vehicleStep1Script: Keep your hands on the steering wheel. Turn on interior lights if nighttime.
scenarioData.vehicleStep1Explanation: Stay calm and visible. Do not make sudden movements.
scenarioData.vehicleStep2Explanation: You have the right to know the reason for the stop.
scenarioData.vehicleStep3Script: I am going to reach for my license and registration now.
scenarioData.vehicleStep3Explanation: Always announce before reaching for anything — this reduces tension and creates a clear verbal record. Hand over only license and registration. You are not required to provide anything else.
scenarioData.vehicleStep4Script: I am exercising my right to remain silent. I do not consent to any searches. I want to speak to a lawyer.
scenarioData.vehicleStep4Explanation: You do not have to answer questions beyond providing license and registration.
scenarioData.vehicleStep5Script: Lock your car and do not consent to searches. You can take a video through the window.
scenarioData.vehicleStep5Explanation: If asked to exit, you must comply, but you can refuse searches.
scenarioData.vehicleOverview: During a traffic stop, you must provide your driver license and vehicle registration. However, you have the right to remain silent beyond that. You do not have to consent to vehicle searches.
scenarioData.vehicleKeyPoint1: ✓ Keep hands visible on steering wheel
scenarioData.vehicleKeyPoint2: ✓ Provide license and registration when asked
scenarioData.vehicleKeyPoint3: ✓ Tell officer before reaching for documents
scenarioData.vehicleKeyPoint4: ✓ You can remain silent beyond basic identification
scenarioData.vehicleKeyPoint5: ✓ You can refuse consent to vehicle searches
scenarioData.vehicleKeyPoint6: ✓ Passengers can ask if they are free to leave
scenarioData.vehicleWarrantJudicialDesc: ICE needs a warrant to search your vehicle without your consent.
scenarioData.vehicleWarrantAdminDesc: Clearly state: "I do not consent to any searches."
scenarioData.vehicleDecision3Question: Did they request to search your vehicle?
scenarioData.vehicleBranch3aScript: I do not consent to any searches of my vehicle.
scenarioData.vehicleBranch3aExplanation: State this once, clearly, and calmly. Even if they search anyway citing probable cause, your refusal is legally significant and on the record. Do not physically resist a search.
scenarioData.vehicleBranch3bScript: Providing these documents does not waive any of my other rights.
scenarioData.vehicleBranch3bExplanation: Handing over license and registration doesn't mean you've consented to anything else. Proceed to step 4 to assert your right to silence and to a lawyer.
scenarioData.vehicleDecision5Question: What happened when asked to exit?
scenarioData.vehicleDecision5OptionA: They searched the vehicle despite my refusal
scenarioData.vehicleDecision5OptionB: They are threatening consequences to pressure consent
scenarioData.vehicleDecision5OptionC: They backed off after I refused
scenarioData.vehicleBranch5aScript: I do not consent to this search. I am not resisting, but I am not consenting.
scenarioData.vehicleBranch5aExplanation: Say this clearly for the record. Do not physically resist. If they searched without consent or probable cause, this can be challenged in court. Note exactly what areas they searched and what they removed.
scenarioData.vehicleBranch5bScript: I do not consent to any searches. I want to speak to a lawyer.
scenarioData.vehicleBranch5bExplanation: Pressure tactics to force consent are common. Repeat your refusal calmly and clearly. If they claim probable cause, they can legally search — but your on-record refusal still matters.
scenarioData.vehicleBranch5cScript: Continue asserting your rights and remain calm until the stop is over.
scenarioData.vehicleBranch5cExplanation: Your refusal worked. Stay calm, keep hands visible. Continue asserting your right to silence and to a lawyer.
scenarioData.vehicleDecision2Question: Are you the driver or a passenger?
scenarioData.vehicleBranch2aScript: Continue to step 3 — you must provide your license, registration, and proof of insurance.
scenarioData.vehicleBranch2aExplanation: As the driver you are legally required to provide these documents when stopped. Always verbally announce before reaching for them.
scenarioData.vehicleBranch2bScript: Am I free to leave? I am a passenger and in most states I am not required to provide identification.
scenarioData.vehicleBranch2bExplanation: Passengers generally have stronger rights than drivers during traffic stops. In most states passengers are not required to provide ID unless there is reasonable suspicion of a crime. You can ask if you are free to leave and may be able to exit the vehicle.
scenarioData.vehicleStep6Script: I will not sign any documents without my lawyer present.
scenarioData.vehicleStep6Explanation: Officers may present consent-to-search forms or other paperwork during a stop. Do not sign anything. Any signature could waive rights you don't realize you are giving up. Wait for your attorney.
scenarioData.borderDesc: Rights at ports of entry and internal checkpoints.
scenarioData.borderStep1Script: Is this a port of entry or an internal checkpoint?
scenarioData.borderStep1Explanation: The type of location determines your rights. Asking the agent puts their answer on record. Your rights at a port of entry (the actual border) are far more limited than at internal checkpoints inside the US.
scenarioData.borderStep2Script: State your citizenship status clearly and briefly. Do not volunteer additional information.
scenarioData.borderStep2Explanation: At the actual border, CBP has broad authority — including vehicle and device searches. Answer basic citizenship questions truthfully. Lying about citizenship is a federal crime.
scenarioData.borderStep3Script: You do not have to answer questions beyond citizenship. You can remain silent.
scenarioData.borderStep3Explanation: Internal checkpoints (within US) have different rules.
scenarioData.borderStep4Script: Am I being detained or am I free to go? I am exercising my right to remain silent.
scenarioData.borderStep4Explanation: At internal checkpoints, you can assert 5th Amendment rights.
scenarioData.borderStep5Script: I do not consent to any searches of my vehicle.
scenarioData.borderStep5Explanation: Even at checkpoints, you can refuse consent to searches.
scenarioData.borderOverview: There are two types of border encounters: actual ports of entry (the border itself) and internal checkpoints (within 100 miles of border). Your rights differ at each location.
scenarioData.borderKeyPoint1: ✓ At ports of entry: Limited rights, must answer citizenship questions
scenarioData.borderKeyPoint2: ✓ At internal checkpoints: More rights, can remain silent beyond citizenship
scenarioData.borderKeyPoint3: ✓ Do not lie about citizenship status
scenarioData.borderKeyPoint4: ✓ You can refuse to show documents beyond driver license when driving
scenarioData.borderKeyPoint5: ✓ You can refuse consent to vehicle searches
scenarioData.borderKeyPoint6: ✓ Document the encounter if safe to do so
scenarioData.borderWarrantJudicialDesc: Limited rights. CBP has broad search authority. Answer basic questions.
scenarioData.borderWarrantAdminDesc: More rights. Can remain silent. Can refuse searches without warrant.
scenarioData.borderDecision1Question: Which type of location is this?
scenarioData.borderDecision1OptionA: Port of entry — the actual border crossing
scenarioData.borderDecision1OptionB: Internal checkpoint — inside the US, within 100 miles of the border
scenarioData.borderBranch1aScript: I understand. I will cooperate with basic entry questions.
scenarioData.borderBranch1aExplanation: At actual ports of entry, CBP has broad authority including the right to search your vehicle and electronic devices. Answer basic citizenship questions truthfully. Do not lie — lying about citizenship is a federal crime.
scenarioData.borderBranch1bScript: I am exercising my right to remain silent beyond confirming my citizenship. Am I free to go?
scenarioData.borderBranch1bExplanation: At internal checkpoints you retain significantly more rights. You may decline most questions beyond citizenship, refuse device searches, and ask if you are free to leave. Proceed through the remaining steps.
scenarioData.borderDecision5Question: What are they requesting to search?
scenarioData.borderBranch5aScript: I do not consent to any searches of my vehicle or belongings.
scenarioData.borderBranch5aExplanation: State non-consent clearly even if they search anyway. Your refusal is on the record and supports any challenge later.
scenarioData.borderBranch5bScript: I do not consent to a search of my electronic device. I want to speak to a lawyer before any device access.
scenarioData.borderBranch5bExplanation: At actual ports of entry, CBP has broad authority to search devices without a warrant and may do so anyway. At internal checkpoints, the law is less settled. State your non-consent clearly for the record. Consider using a travel phone with minimal data at borders. Officers generally cannot compel biometric unlocking (fingerprint or Face ID) in most US jurisdictions.
scenarioData.borderStep6Script: I will not sign any documents without my lawyer present.
scenarioData.borderStep6Explanation: At the border you may be presented with voluntary departure forms (I-407), withdrawal of application for admission, or other documents that permanently waive rights and the ability to appeal removal. Never sign without an attorney reviewing first. A signature here can affect immigration status for years.
scenarioData.workplaceDesc: ICE visits to employment sites. Don't run, stay silent.
scenarioData.workplaceStep1Script: Running can be used against you. Stay where you are.
scenarioData.workplaceStep1Explanation: Fleeing can be used as evidence. Remain calm.
scenarioData.workplaceStep2Script: I am exercising my right to remain silent. I want to speak to a lawyer.
scenarioData.workplaceStep2Explanation: You have the right to remain silent at work.
scenarioData.workplaceStep3Script: I do not consent to showing any documents without a lawyer present.
scenarioData.workplaceStep3Explanation: You do not have to show work authorization documents to ICE.
scenarioData.workplaceStep4Explanation: You may be able to leave if not detained.
scenarioData.workplaceStep5Script: ICE needs a judicial warrant to enter non-public areas of the workplace.
scenarioData.workplaceStep5Explanation: Private areas of workplace have same protections as a home.
scenarioData.workplaceOverview: ICE may visit workplaces. In public areas, they have more access. In private/non-public areas, they need a judicial warrant. You have the right to remain silent and ask for a lawyer.
scenarioData.workplaceKeyPoint2: ✓ Exercise your right to remain silent
scenarioData.workplaceKeyPoint3: ✓ Do not show documents without a lawyer
scenarioData.workplaceKeyPoint4: ✓ Ask if you are free to leave
scenarioData.workplaceKeyPoint5: ✓ ICE needs a judicial warrant for non-public workplace areas
scenarioData.workplaceKeyPoint6: ✓ You can refuse to answer questions
scenarioData.workplaceWarrantJudicialDesc: ICE needs a judicial warrant to enter private workplace areas (break rooms, offices).
scenarioData.workplaceWarrantAdminDesc: ICE may access public areas (lobby, customer areas) without a warrant.
scenarioData.workplaceBranch4aScript: Walk away calmly. Do not run. Alert a trusted coworker quietly if it is safe to do so.
scenarioData.workplaceBranch4aExplanation: Leave immediately and calmly. Contact your attorney and trusted contact right away. You are not obligated to stay.
scenarioData.workplaceBranch4bScript: What is the legal basis for my detention? I am exercising my right to remain silent and want to speak to a lawyer.
scenarioData.workplaceBranch4bExplanation: If detained, they need a legal basis. Ask clearly — it goes on record. Whether you are in a public or non-public area affects your rights significantly. Proceed to step 5.
scenarioData.workplaceBranch4cScript: I am taking that as consent to leave. I am going now.
scenarioData.workplaceBranch4cExplanation: A non-answer can be treated as implicit permission to leave. Walk away calmly and contact your attorney immediately.
scenarioData.workplaceDecision5OptionA: Public area — lobby, sales floor, customer area
scenarioData.workplaceDecision5OptionB: Non-public area — break room, back office, warehouse, kitchen
scenarioData.workplaceBranch5aScript: I am exercising my right to remain silent. I want to speak to a lawyer.
scenarioData.workplaceBranch5aExplanation: In public workplace areas ICE has greater access and can interact with anyone present. Your right to silence still applies — do not answer questions about immigration status or anything else.
scenarioData.workplaceBranch5bScript: This is a non-public area. ICE needs a judicial warrant signed by a judge to enter here. Do you have one?
scenarioData.workplaceBranch5bExplanation: Non-public workplace areas carry the same constitutional protections as a private home. An administrative warrant (ICE-signed) does NOT authorize entry. Your employer also has the right to deny ICE access to these areas.
scenarioData.workplaceDecision3OptionA: My employer is refusing ICE entry or actively helping me
scenarioData.workplaceDecision3OptionB: My employer appears to be cooperating with ICE
scenarioData.workplaceBranch3aScript: My employer is exercising their right to refuse ICE access to this non-public area without a judicial warrant.
scenarioData.workplaceBranch3aExplanation: Employers have the legal right to deny ICE access to non-public areas without a judicial warrant. If your employer is actively blocking ICE, support this — do not contradict them by opening doors or producing documents.
scenarioData.workplaceBranch3bScript: I am exercising my individual right to remain silent regardless of my employer's actions. I want to speak to a lawyer.
scenarioData.workplaceBranch3bExplanation: Even if your employer cooperates with ICE, your individual constitutional rights remain fully intact. An employer cannot consent to search your person, waive your right to silence, or speak on your behalf in a legal proceeding. Your rights are yours alone.
scenarioData.workplaceStep6Script: I will not sign any employment verification forms or immigration documents without my lawyer present.
scenarioData.workplaceStep6Explanation: ICE workplace raids often include I-9 audit demands, employment eligibility re-verification forms, and other documents. Signing any of these without legal review could waive rights or create documentation that harms your case. Your employer may pressure you to sign — you are not legally required to do so without counsel.
scenarioData.protestDesc: Best practices and legal boundaries for peaceful assembly.
scenarioData.protestStep1Script: I am peacefully exercising my First Amendment right to assemble.
scenarioData.protestStep1Explanation: The First Amendment protects peaceful protest in public spaces.
scenarioData.protestStep2Script: Remain on sidewalks, parks, and public plazas. Do not block entrances or traffic.
scenarioData.protestStep2Explanation: Public spaces are protected. Private property requires permission.
scenarioData.protestStep3Script: I am exercising my constitutional right to peaceful assembly. Am I being detained or am I free to go?
scenarioData.protestStep3Explanation: Calmly assert your rights. Ask if you are being detained.
scenarioData.protestStep4Script: What is the legal basis for this dispersal order? How much time do I have to comply?
scenarioData.protestStep4Explanation: Asking on record is not defiance — it's documentation. Note the time, the reason given, and the officer's name or badge. Then comply within the timeframe. Failure to disperse after a lawful order can result in arrest.
scenarioData.protestStep5Script: I am exercising my right to remain silent. I want a lawyer.
scenarioData.protestStep5Explanation: Do not resist. Go limp if necessary. Assert your rights verbally.
scenarioData.protestOverview: The First Amendment protects your right to peacefully assemble and protest. This includes marches, rallies, and demonstrations in public spaces. However, there are legal boundaries you should understand.
scenarioData.protestKeyPoint1: ✓ You can protest on public sidewalks and parks
scenarioData.protestKeyPoint2: ✓ You can photograph and record at protests
scenarioData.protestKeyPoint3: ✓ Police cannot prevent you from protesting based on content
scenarioData.protestKeyPoint4: ✓ You may need permits for large gatherings or blocking streets
scenarioData.protestKeyPoint5: ✓ Counter-protesters have the same rights as you
scenarioData.protestKeyPoint6: ✓ You can be arrested for blocking traffic or trespassing
scenarioData.protestWarrantJudicialDesc: Peaceful assembly, carrying signs, chanting, marching on sidewalks, recording.
scenarioData.protestWarrantAdminDesc: Violence, property destruction, blocking emergency vehicles, trespassing.
scenarioData.protestBranch3aScript: Walk away calmly. Keep your hands visible. Do not run.
scenarioData.protestBranch3aExplanation: You are free to return to the protest or leave the area. Do not run — stay calm and composed as you leave.
scenarioData.protestBranch3bScript: What is the legal basis for my detention? I am exercising my right to remain silent and want to speak to a lawyer.
scenarioData.protestBranch3bExplanation: At a protest, police must have reasonable suspicion of a specific crime to detain you — peaceful assembly alone is not sufficient. Ask the legal basis and note their answer. Proceed to step 4.
scenarioData.protestBranch3cScript: I am taking your non-answer as consent to leave. I am going now.
scenarioData.protestBranch3cExplanation: A non-answer or evasion can be treated as implicit permission to leave. Say this clearly and walk away calmly. Do not run.
scenarioData.protestDecision5Question: How are they making the arrest?
scenarioData.protestDecision5OptionB: They are using force or it is becoming violent
scenarioData.protestBranch5aScript: I am not resisting. I am invoking my right to remain silent and want a lawyer.
scenarioData.protestBranch5aExplanation: Comply with the physical arrest while clearly asserting your rights verbally. Remember: badge numbers, time, and location. You will have the opportunity to challenge the arrest later.
scenarioData.protestBranch5bScript: I am not resisting. Stop. I need medical attention.
scenarioData.protestBranch5bExplanation: Do not fight back — it escalates danger and adds charges. Shout 'I am not resisting' loudly so witnesses hear. If you are injured, demand medical attention immediately and photograph injuries as soon as you are able.
scenarioData.protestDecision2Question: Are there witnesses or legal observers nearby?
scenarioData.protestDecision2OptionA: Yes — legal observers or ACLU monitors are present
scenarioData.protestDecision2OptionB: Bystanders are present but no formal legal observers
scenarioData.protestBranch2aScript: I would like a legal observer to witness this interaction.
scenarioData.protestBranch2aExplanation: Legal observers at protests (often wearing green hats, ACLU vests, or NLG badges) are trained to document rights violations. Make your request loudly and clearly. Their documentation can be used in your defense and in formal complaints.
scenarioData.protestBranch2bScript: Can someone please witness this? Note the officer's badge number and agency.
scenarioData.protestBranch2bExplanation: Any witness matters. Calling for witnesses loudly and calmly deters misconduct and creates additional documentation. You are not directing anyone to interfere — only to observe.
scenarioData.protestBranch2cScript: State your name and location aloud if recording. Note badge numbers, agency, and time.
scenarioData.protestBranch2cExplanation: If no witnesses are present, verbal documentation for any recording device is important. State identifying details clearly. Note badge numbers, agency markings, vehicle descriptions, and time.
scenarioData.recordingDesc: When and how you can legally document ICE activity.
scenarioData.recordingStep1Script: I am exercising my First Amendment right to record in a public space.
scenarioData.recordingStep1Explanation: Recording police and ICE in public is constitutionally protected.
scenarioData.recordingStep2Script: Stay at least 10 feet away. Do not interfere with their activities.
scenarioData.recordingStep2Explanation: You can record but cannot obstruct law enforcement duties.
scenarioData.recordingStep3Script: I am not interfering. I am recording from a public space which is my constitutional right.
scenarioData.recordingStep3Explanation: Calmly assert your rights. Do not argue or become confrontational.
scenarioData.recordingStep4Script: You cannot compel me to delete this footage.
scenarioData.recordingStep4Explanation: Officers cannot legally order you to delete recordings or seize your phone without a warrant. This footage may be critical evidence. Use apps with auto-upload (like SafeNeighbor's vault or Google Photos backup) so footage is preserved even if your phone is taken.
scenarioData.recordingStep5Script: Note: time, location, badge numbers, agency, vehicle descriptions, and what actions were taken.
scenarioData.recordingStep5Explanation: This information helps protect community members and holds agencies accountable.
scenarioData.recordingOverview: The First Amendment protects your right to record police and ICE agents in public spaces. This includes sidewalks, parks, and other public areas. You cannot be arrested simply for recording, but you must not interfere with their duties.
scenarioData.recordingKeyPoint1: ✓ You CAN record law enforcement in public spaces
scenarioData.recordingKeyPoint2: ✓ Keep a safe distance (10+ feet recommended)
scenarioData.recordingKeyPoint3: ✓ Do not physically interfere with operations
scenarioData.recordingKeyPoint5: ✓ Officers need a warrant to seize your phone
scenarioData.recordingKeyPoint6: ✓ Back up footage to the cloud immediately
scenarioData.recordingWarrantJudicialDesc: Record openly in public. Assert your First Amendment rights. Back up footage to cloud.
scenarioData.recordingWarrantAdminDesc: Do not interfere. Do not trespass on private property. Do not obstruct operations.
scenarioData.recordingDecision3Question: What happened when you asserted your right?
scenarioData.recordingDecision3OptionA: They threatened to arrest me for recording
scenarioData.recordingDecision3OptionB: They tried to take or seize my phone
scenarioData.recordingDecision3OptionC: They moved me back but I can still record
scenarioData.recordingBranch3aScript: I am not interfering. Recording in a public space is my constitutional right.
scenarioData.recordingBranch3aExplanation: Threatening arrest for lawful recording is unlawful. If your physical safety is at genuine risk, prioritize your safety over footage. Note everything you remember immediately after the encounter.
scenarioData.recordingBranch3bScript: You cannot seize my phone without a warrant. I do not consent to this.
scenarioData.recordingBranch3bExplanation: Officers need a judicial warrant to seize your device. If they take it by force, do not physically resist — but document the seizure and contact an attorney immediately. Your footage may already be backed up to cloud.
scenarioData.recordingBranch3cScript: Moving back. I am continuing to document from a safe distance.
scenarioData.recordingBranch3cExplanation: Comply with reasonable distance requests while continuing to record. Capture badge numbers, agency markings, and vehicle plates as you move.
scenarioData.sensitiveDesc: ICE enforcement at schools, hospitals, churches, and shelters.
scenarioData.sensitiveStep1Script: Is this a school, hospital, place of worship, or shelter?
scenarioData.sensitiveStep1Explanation: These are designated sensitive locations where ICE was historically restricted from conducting enforcement. While current policy has weakened these protections, identifying the location type and asserting the policy on record still matters — and facility staff often have trained protocols.
scenarioData.sensitiveDecision1Question: What type of location is this?
scenarioData.sensitiveDecision1OptionC: Place of worship — church, mosque, synagogue, temple
scenarioData.sensitiveDecision1OptionD: Shelter, food bank, or social services facility
scenarioData.sensitiveBranch1aScript: This is an educational institution. DHS policy designates schools as sensitive locations. I am requesting you comply with sensitive location guidelines.
scenarioData.sensitiveBranch1aExplanation: Schools are designated sensitive locations. Alert school administration immediately. The Supreme Court's Plyler v. Doe guarantees K-12 education regardless of immigration status. Children present have particular vulnerability — keep children calm and away from the situation.
scenarioData.sensitiveBranch1bScript: This is a medical facility. DHS policy designates hospitals as sensitive locations. I am requesting you comply with sensitive location guidelines. I have a medical need.
scenarioData.sensitiveBranch1bExplanation: Hospitals are designated sensitive locations. Asserting a medical need adds urgency and may provide additional protection. Alert hospital security and medical staff immediately — hospitals often have legal teams and specific protocols for ICE encounters.
scenarioData.sensitiveBranch1cScript: This is a place of worship. DHS policy designates houses of worship as sensitive locations. I am requesting you comply with sensitive location guidelines.
scenarioData.sensitiveBranch1cExplanation: Churches, mosques, synagogues, and other religious institutions are designated sensitive locations. If this institution has declared itself a sanctuary space, state that clearly. Alert the pastor, imam, rabbi, or facility administrator immediately.
scenarioData.sensitiveBranch1dScript: This is a social services facility. DHS policy designates shelters as sensitive locations. I am requesting you comply with sensitive location guidelines.
scenarioData.sensitiveBranch1dExplanation: Shelters, food banks, and social service facilities serving vulnerable populations are designated sensitive locations. Alert facility staff immediately — many have trained legal protocols and relationships with immigration attorneys.
scenarioData.sensitiveStep2Script: This is a designated sensitive location under DHS policy. You are required to obtain supervisory approval before conducting enforcement here.
scenarioData.sensitiveStep2Explanation: Even though current administration has significantly weakened enforcement of sensitive location policies, stating this creates a record. Officers are still technically required to obtain supervisory approval. Stating it loudly may also alert staff and bystanders who can document and respond.
scenarioData.sensitiveStep3Script: Alert the principal, hospital administrator, pastor, shelter director, or security personnel immediately.
scenarioData.sensitiveStep3Explanation: Facility administrators can refuse ICE entry to non-public areas without a judicial warrant. Many schools, hospitals, and churches have legal teams and trained protocols. The more staff who know what is happening, the better. Administrators can also contact legal observers and attorneys.
scenarioData.sensitiveStep4Script: I am exercising my right to remain silent. I want to speak to a lawyer.
scenarioData.sensitiveStep4Explanation: Your individual constitutional rights apply fully regardless of location. Do not answer questions about immigration status or any other topic. Your sensitive location protections and your individual rights work together — assert both.
scenarioData.sensitiveStep5Script: Note agent names, badge numbers, agency, time, who else was present, and exactly what was said.
scenarioData.sensitiveStep5Explanation: Documentation at sensitive locations is especially important. It supports potential complaints to DHS Office of Inspector General, DHS CRCL (Civil Rights and Civil Liberties), your congressional representatives, and civil rights organizations. A sensitive location violation is a significant and reportable event.
scenarioData.sensitiveOverview: ICE historically designated schools, hospitals, churches, and shelters as sensitive locations where enforcement operations were to be avoided. The current administration has significantly weakened these protections and directed ICE to resume enforcement at these sites. However, the policy designation technically remains in effect — ICE is still supposed to obtain supervisory approval. Knowing how to assert this policy, how to alert facility staff, and how to document violations can make a meaningful difference.
scenarioData.sensitiveKeyPoint1: ✓ Schools, hospitals, houses of worship, and shelters are designated sensitive locations
scenarioData.sensitiveKeyPoint2: ✓ ICE technically requires supervisory approval before enforcement at these locations
scenarioData.sensitiveKeyPoint3: ✓ Current policy has significantly weakened these protections — do not rely on them alone
scenarioData.sensitiveKeyPoint4: ✓ Alert facility administration immediately — many have trained legal protocols
scenarioData.sensitiveKeyPoint5: ✓ Your individual constitutional rights apply fully regardless of location
scenarioData.sensitiveKeyPoint6: ✓ Document everything — sensitive location violations support civil rights complaints
scenarioData.sensitiveWarrantJudicialDesc: The current administration has directed ICE to resume enforcement at sensitive locations. Do not rely on this designation as full protection — assert it, alert staff, and use all available rights.
scenarioData.sensitiveWarrantAdminDesc: ICE still technically requires supervisory approval at these locations. Alert facility staff, assert the policy on record, and document everything to support potential complaints.

postEncounterData.detainedReleasedDesc: You were detained by ICE/DHS and have been released. The first 24-72 hours are critical — evidence fades, legal deadlines start, and without guidance people miss court dates or lose their case.
postEncounterData.familyTakenDesc: A family member has been detained by ICE. Your priority is finding where they are, getting them legal help, and activating your family emergency plan.
postEncounterData.agentsLeftDesc: ICE/DHS came to your door but left without entering. You exercised your rights — now document what happened and prepare for the possibility they may return.
postEncounterData.documentNowDrContent: Memory degrades fast after a traumatic event. Write down everything you remember right now — names, badge numbers, what was said, what happened. This becomes critical evidence for your attorney and any future complaint.
postEncounterData.documentNowDrCheck1: Write down names and badge numbers of all agents you saw
postEncounterData.documentNowDrCheck2: Note the exact date, time, and location of your detention
postEncounterData.documentNowDrCheck3: Describe what agents said to you and what you said back
postEncounterData.documentNowDrCheck4: Photograph any injuries, bruises, or property damage
postEncounterData.documentNowDrCheck5: Write down names and contact info of any witnesses
postEncounterData.documentNowDrCheck6: Save all paperwork they gave you (NTA, bond papers, receipts)
postEncounterData.documentNowDrCheck7: Note which facility you were held at and for how long
postEncounterData.documentNowDrCheck8: Document conditions of detention (food, water, medical care, temperature)
postEncounterData.documentNowDrCheck9: Record if you were denied access to an attorney or phone call
postEncounterData.legalHelpDrContent: You likely received a Notice to Appear (NTA) with a court date. Without an attorney, removal rates are dramatically higher. Immigration court does not provide free lawyers — you must find your own. Start immediately.
postEncounterData.legalHelpDrCheck1: Contact an immigration attorney as soon as possible
postEncounterData.legalHelpDrCheck2: Call the National Immigration Detention Hotline: 1-833-560-0927
postEncounterData.legalHelpDrCheck3: Contact your local legal aid organization
postEncounterData.legalHelpDrCheck4: Request a list of pro bono attorneys from the immigration court
postEncounterData.legalHelpDrCheck5: Gather all immigration documents for your attorney
postEncounterData.legalHelpDrCheck6: Ask your attorney about bond reduction hearing options
postEncounterData.legalHelpDrCheck7: If you cannot afford an attorney, contact NILC or local immigrant rights orgs
postEncounterData.bondCourtDrContent: Missing a court date results in an automatic removal (deportation) order. Your NTA paperwork contains your court date and location. Understanding the process can be the difference between staying and being removed.
postEncounterData.bondCourtDrCheck1: Locate your NTA and note your court date, time, and location
postEncounterData.bondCourtDrCheck2: Identify which immigration court has jurisdiction over your case
postEncounterData.bondCourtDrCheck3: Understand your bond conditions and any reporting requirements
postEncounterData.bondCourtDrCheck4: Set multiple reminders for your court date — show up early
postEncounterData.bondCourtDrCheck5: Prepare all documents your attorney needs before the hearing
postEncounterData.bondCourtDrCheck6: Know that you can request a continuance if you need more time to find an attorney
postEncounterData.bondCourtDrCheck7: Understand that immigration court is civil, not criminal — but consequences are just as serious
postEncounterData.preserveEvidenceDrContent: Recordings, photos, and documents lose legal value if edited or mishandled. Chain of custody matters in court. Back up everything now and do not modify originals.
postEncounterData.preserveEvidenceDrCheck1: Back up all recordings to a secure location (Google Drive, email to attorney)
postEncounterData.preserveEvidenceDrCheck2: Do NOT edit, crop, or modify any video or audio recordings
postEncounterData.preserveEvidenceDrCheck3: Screenshot and save all metadata (timestamps, GPS coordinates)
postEncounterData.preserveEvidenceDrCheck4: Email copies of all evidence to your attorney immediately
postEncounterData.preserveEvidenceDrCheck5: Note the chain of custody for each piece of evidence (who had it, when)
postEncounterData.preserveEvidenceDrCheck6: If you used SafeNeighbor to record, share the encrypted backup with your attorney
postEncounterData.preserveEvidenceDrCheck7: Preserve text messages, call logs, and any communication with agents
postEncounterData.fileComplaintDrContent: If agents violated your rights — entered without a judicial warrant, used excessive force, denied you access to an attorney, or made threats — you can file federal complaints. Most people don't know these channels exist.
postEncounterData.fileComplaintDrCheck1: File a complaint with DHS Office of Inspector General (OIG)
postEncounterData.fileComplaintDrCheck2: File a complaint with DHS CRCL (Office for Civil Rights and Civil Liberties)
postEncounterData.fileComplaintDrCheck3: Contact your state Attorney General's office
postEncounterData.fileComplaintDrCheck4: Report the incident to the ACLU
postEncounterData.fileComplaintDrCheck5: Document the complaint filing date and case number for your records
postEncounterData.fileComplaintDrCheck6: Ask your attorney about potential civil rights claims (Section 1983)
postEncounterData.findThemFtTitle: FIND WHERE THEY ARE BEING HELD
postEncounterData.findThemFtContent: ICE can transfer detainees between facilities without notice. The sooner you locate them, the sooner you can get them an attorney and begin the bond process. Use the ICE Online Detainee Locator and call the detention hotline.
postEncounterData.findThemFtCheck1: Call the National Immigration Detention Hotline: 1-833-560-0927
postEncounterData.findThemFtCheck2: Use the ICE Online Detainee Locator at locator.ice.gov
postEncounterData.findThemFtCheck3: Call the local ICE ERO (Enforcement and Removal Operations) field office
postEncounterData.findThemFtCheck4: Check if they were transferred to a different facility
postEncounterData.findThemFtCheck5: Note the facility name, address, phone number, and visitation hours
postEncounterData.findThemFtCheck6: Ask about their alien registration number (A-number) if you don't have it
postEncounterData.findThemFtCheck7: Find out if they have been seen by a judge yet
postEncounterData.legalHelpFtContent: Detained people have the right to an attorney, but the government will NOT provide one. You need to find and hire one on their behalf. Time matters — bond eligibility decisions happen fast.
postEncounterData.legalHelpFtCheck1: Contact an immigration attorney on their behalf
postEncounterData.legalHelpFtCheck2: Call local legal aid organizations for referrals
postEncounterData.legalHelpFtCheck3: Contact NILC or local immigrant rights organizations
postEncounterData.legalHelpFtCheck4: Gather their immigration documents for the attorney
postEncounterData.legalHelpFtCheck5: Ask the attorney about bond eligibility and hearing timeline
postEncounterData.legalHelpFtCheck6: Find out if they qualify for a bond hearing or must wait
postEncounterData.legalHelpFtCheck7: If they cannot afford an attorney, ask about pro bono representation
postEncounterData.poaActivationFtContent: If you prepared a Power of Attorney through the Family Preparedness Kit, now is when it activates. This gives you legal authority to manage finances, childcare, school authorization, and other critical matters on their behalf.
postEncounterData.poaActivationFtCheck1: Locate the Power of Attorney document
postEncounterData.poaActivationFtCheck2: Notify banks and financial institutions with a copy of the POA
postEncounterData.poaActivationFtCheck3: Contact your children's school with custody/pickup authorization
postEncounterData.poaActivationFtCheck4: Arrange childcare per your family emergency plan
postEncounterData.poaActivationFtCheck5: Access shared financial accounts as authorized
postEncounterData.poaActivationFtCheck6: Notify your employer if needed (FMLA, leave of absence)
postEncounterData.poaActivationFtCheck7: If no POA exists, consult an attorney about emergency guardianship
postEncounterData.notifyNetworkFtContent: Activate your trusted contacts, community organizations, and faith communities. You should not go through this alone. Your support network can help with childcare, legal fund coordination, and emotional support.
postEncounterData.notifyNetworkFtCheck1: Alert all trusted contacts from your emergency plan
postEncounterData.notifyNetworkFtCheck2: Notify community organizations (mutual aid, immigrant rights groups)
postEncounterData.notifyNetworkFtCheck3: Contact religious or faith community leaders for support
postEncounterData.notifyNetworkFtCheck4: Set up a communication chain for updates on the case
postEncounterData.notifyNetworkFtCheck5: Consider a GoFundMe or community collection for legal fees
postEncounterData.notifyNetworkFtCheck6: Ask for help with daily logistics (children, meals, transportation)
postEncounterData.documentFtContent: Even though you weren't the one detained, document everything you witnessed. Your testimony and evidence can be critical for their legal defense and any complaints against rights violations.
postEncounterData.documentFtCheck1: Write down everything you witnessed — times, agents, actions
postEncounterData.documentFtCheck2: Save any recordings, photos, or videos of the encounter
postEncounterData.documentFtCheck3: Note names and contact info of any witnesses
postEncounterData.documentFtCheck4: Keep copies of all paperwork agents left behind
postEncounterData.documentFtCheck5: Document any property damage or items taken
postEncounterData.documentFtCheck6: Record any statements agents made about the reason for arrest
postEncounterData.documentVisitAlContent: Even though agents left, documenting the visit creates a record that could matter later — for your attorney, for community awareness, and in case they return with a warrant.
postEncounterData.documentVisitAlCheck1: Write down the exact date, time, and duration of the visit
postEncounterData.documentVisitAlCheck2: Note how many agents were present and their appearance
postEncounterData.documentVisitAlCheck3: Record what they said and what you said in response
postEncounterData.documentVisitAlCheck4: Save any papers, cards, or notices they left behind
postEncounterData.documentVisitAlCheck5: Check for any surveillance vehicles lingering nearby after they left
postEncounterData.documentVisitAlCheck6: Note badge numbers, vehicle descriptions, or license plate numbers
postEncounterData.documentVisitAlCheck7: Report the visit to SafeNeighbor Community Reports
postEncounterData.followupPatternsAlContent: ICE may return. Understanding common patterns helps you prepare. Return visits often happen in the early morning (5-7 AM) or late evening. They may also canvas your workplace or neighborhood.
postEncounterData.followupPatternsAlCheck1: Be alert for return visits, especially early morning (5-7 AM) or late evening
postEncounterData.followupPatternsAlCheck2: Know that ICE may canvas your neighborhood or ask neighbors about you
postEncounterData.followupPatternsAlCheck3: Be aware they may approach you at your workplace instead
postEncounterData.followupPatternsAlCheck4: They may return with a judicial warrant next time — know the difference
postEncounterData.followupPatternsAlCheck5: Alert trusted neighbors if you feel safe doing so
postEncounterData.followupPatternsAlCheck6: Check with community organizations if others in your area had similar visits
postEncounterData.followupPatternsAlCheck7: Consider varying your daily routine temporarily
postEncounterData.fortifyPrepAlContent: This experience is a wake-up call. Use it to reinforce your family plan, practice your scripts, and make sure everyone in your household knows what to do if agents return.
postEncounterData.fortifyPrepAlCheck1: Review and update your Family Preparedness Kit
postEncounterData.fortifyPrepAlCheck2: Ensure your Power of Attorney is current and notarized
postEncounterData.fortifyPrepAlCheck3: Update your trusted contacts with details of today's visit
postEncounterData.fortifyPrepAlCheck4: Practice door scripts with all family members again
postEncounterData.fortifyPrepAlCheck5: Make sure everyone in the household knows: DO NOT OPEN THE DOOR
postEncounterData.fortifyPrepAlCheck6: Consider installing a doorbell camera or security camera
postEncounterData.fortifyPrepAlCheck7: Attend a local Know Your Rights workshop
postEncounterData.consultAttorneyAlContent: A return visit may come with a judicial warrant. Consulting an immigration attorney now — before you're in a crisis — can help you understand your options and prepare your case proactively.
postEncounterData.consultAttorneyAlCheck1: Schedule a consultation with an immigration attorney
postEncounterData.consultAttorneyAlCheck2: Bring documentation of the visit (your notes, any papers left behind)
postEncounterData.consultAttorneyAlCheck3: Ask about your specific immigration status and vulnerabilities
postEncounterData.consultAttorneyAlCheck4: Understand what a judicial warrant vs. administrative warrant means for you
postEncounterData.consultAttorneyAlCheck5: Ask about voluntary departure vs. removal proceedings
postEncounterData.consultAttorneyAlCheck6: Get the attorney's emergency contact number for future incidents
postEncounterData.courtRightsContent: Immigration court is civil, not criminal — but the consequences are just as life-altering. Understanding the system gives you and your attorney a better chance. These are the fundamentals everyone should know.
postEncounterData.courtRightsInfo1: Immigration court is civil, not criminal — but you can still be detained throughout proceedings
postEncounterData.courtRightsInfo2: You have the right to an attorney, but the government will NOT provide one for free
postEncounterData.courtRightsInfo3: You can request a continuance (delay) to find legal representation
postEncounterData.courtRightsInfo4: Bond hearings determine if you can be released while your case proceeds
postEncounterData.courtRightsInfo5: You can appeal decisions to the Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA)
postEncounterData.courtRightsInfo6: NEVER miss a court date — it results in an automatic removal (deportation) order
postEncounterData.courtRightsInfo7: You have the right to review all evidence the government has against you
postEncounterData.courtRightsInfo8: You can apply for relief from removal (asylum, cancellation of removal, etc.)
postEncounterData.resourcesContent: These organizations provide legal help, detainee location services, know-your-rights information, and complaint filing. Save these numbers now.

rightsCard.title: Know Your Rights Card
rightsCard.subtitle: A wallet-size card with your essential rights. Screenshot it, print it, or share it. Works fully offline in your language.
rightsCard.right1: DO NOT OPEN THE DOOR if an immigration agent is knocking on the door.
rightsCard.right2: DO NOT ANSWER ANY QUESTIONS from an immigration agent if they try to talk to you. You have the right to remain silent.
rightsCard.right3: DO NOT SIGN ANYTHING without first speaking to a lawyer. You have the right to speak with a lawyer.
rightsCard.right4: If you are outside of your home, ask the agent if you are free to leave and if they say yes, leave calmly.
rightsCard.right5: SHOW THIS CARD TO THE AGENT. If you are inside of your home, show the card through the window or slide it under the door.
rightsCard.assertion1: I do not wish to speak with you, answer your questions, or sign or hand you any documents based on my 5th Amendment rights under the United States Constitution.
rightsCard.assertion2: I do not give you permission to enter my home based on my 4th Amendment rights under the United States Constitution unless you have a warrant to enter, signed by a judge or magistrate with my name on it that you slide under the door.
rightsCard.assertion3: I do not give you permission to search any of my belongings based on my 4th Amendment rights.
rightsCard.assertion4: I choose to exercise my constitutional rights.
rightsCard.agentFooter: These cards are available to citizens and noncitizens alike.
rightsCard.disclaimer: Not legal advice. Consult a licensed attorney.

faq.title: Community FAQ
faq.subtitle: Answers to common questions about SafeNeighbor, privacy, and your safety.
faq.generalA1: SafeNeighbor is a privacy-first web platform designed to empower communities through real-time safety reporting and civil rights education. We provide tools to document law enforcement activity and access legal scripts for high-stress encounters.
faq.generalA2: No. SafeNeighbor is an independent, community-driven resource. We are not affiliated with any government agency or law enforcement body. Our loyalty is entirely to the privacy and safety of our users.
faq.generalQ3: How does the reporting map work?
faq.generalA3: When a user sees enforcement activity, they can pin a report. This report is then visible to other users in the area, allowing neighbors to make informed decisions about their travel and safety in real-time. Reports do not require an account, name, email, or phone number. Report locations are generalized before storage, and server-side controls are used to reduce spam and abuse. Network metadata may still be processed for operational protections like rate limiting, but it is not attached to the public report that other users see.
faq.privacyQ1: Do I need to create an account to use SafeNeighbor?
faq.privacyA1: No. We do not require names, emails, phone numbers, or social media logins. You can access the map and all legal scripts completely anonymously.
faq.privacyQ2: How do you protect my location?
faq.privacyA2: We do not track you. While the app uses your device's GPS to show you local reports, that data is processed locally on your phone. We do not store a history of your movements on our servers.
faq.privacyA3: SafeNeighbor uses two different privacy models. Recordings, backups, and other sensitive device data are protected with local encryption and keys you control. Community reports use a privacy-preserving, data-minimizing model instead: direct identifiers are stripped before upload, locations are generalized, and no account, name, email, or phone number is required to use the map.
faq.privacyA4: Yes. If you use the platform to document an encounter, the file is stored in your encrypted local vault and any backup is encrypted before upload. You hold the key. Without your explicit action to share it, the recording remains inaccessible to third parties.
faq.legalQ1: Does using this app make me a target?
faq.legalA1: Exercising your constitutional rights and staying informed is legal. Because we do not collect identifying information, using the app does not create a digital paper trail linking your identity to your activity.
faq.legalQ2: Are the "Know Your Rights" scripts legally binding?
faq.legalA2: The scripts are based on established Constitutional law (such as the 4th and 5th Amendments). However, they are for educational purposes and do not constitute formal legal advice. We always recommend consulting with a civil rights attorney for specific legal cases.
faq.legalQ3: What should I do if a report is inaccurate?
faq.legalA3: Community reporting relies on mutual trust. Users can verify or flag reports. If a report receives multiple flags for being inaccurate, it is automatically removed from the map to ensure the community has the most reliable information possible.
faq.philosophyQ1: Why is there Stoic philosophy on the site?
faq.philosophyA1: We believe that safety requires a clear mind. Stoic principles teach us to focus on what we can control — our actions, our preparation, and our duty to our neighbors — even in chaotic situations.
faq.disclaimer: This FAQ is for informational purposes only and does not constitute legal advice. Consult a licensed attorney for specific legal situations.

techSecurity.title: Security & Privacy Architecture
techSecurity.subtitle: We don't just promise privacy — we enforce it through our software architecture.
techSecurity.introText: Our system is built on the principle of Data Minimization — if we don't have it, we can't lose it, and we can't be forced to share it.
techSecurity.zkaDesc: We design the app to keep sensitive data local when possible and to store as little identifying information as possible. In practice, that means:
techSecurity.zkaNoAccountsDesc: There is no registration process. We do not store usernames, passwords, emails, or phone numbers.
techSecurity.zkaClientSideDesc: Whenever possible, logic (such as location filtering) happens in your browser's memory, not on our servers.
techSecurity.cryptoDesc: SafeNeighbor separates public-warning data from sensitive evidence. Community reports are privacy-preserving and generalized, while recordings and vault data stay protected with device-controlled encryption.
techSecurity.cryptoMetadataDesc: Our system automatically strips EXIF data and metadata from any uploaded images or reports to prevent digital fingerprinting of your device.
techSecurity.cryptoTransitDesc: All data is transmitted via TLS 1.3 (Transport Layer Security), protecting your information from Man-in-the-Middle (MITM) attacks by third parties or ISPs.
techSecurity.cryptoAtRestDesc: Any identifiers necessary for platform stability are processed through one-way cryptographic hashes. We see a string of random characters, not your identity.
techSecurity.locationDesc: SafeNeighbor uses a Non-Persistent Location Model:
techSecurity.locationGeofenceDesc: Your device's precise coordinates are used locally to calculate which alerts are relevant to you.
techSecurity.locationJitterDesc: Public pins on the map are slightly offset or "jittered." This prevents anyone from determining the exact location from which a report was filed, protecting the whistleblower's precise location.
techSecurity.trackingNoAdsDesc: We do not use Facebook Pixels, Google Tag Manager, or any other third-party tracking scripts that phone home to big-tech advertising platforms.
techSecurity.trackingAnalyticsDesc: We use privacy-respecting, cookieless analytics that aggregate total site visits without tracking individual user journeys.
techSecurity.subpoenaDesc: Our legal strategy is a technical one: keep identifying data and sensitive content to a minimum. We do not require user accounts for the reporting map, we do not attach names or contact details to public reports, and recordings remain encrypted with keys that stay under user control.
techSecurity.specsEncryptionValue: AES-256 (at rest), AES-KW key wrapping (PIN), TLS 1.3 (in transit)
techSecurity.specsArchitectureValue: Client-side encryption for device data, generalized reports, no account required
techSecurity.specsAuditValue: We welcome community review of our methodology to ensure we are meeting the highest standards of civic-tech safety.
techSecurity.disclaimer: This documentation is provided for transparency purposes. Our security architecture is subject to continuous improvement. All claims herein reflect our current implementation.

guardiansManual.title: The Guardian's Manual
guardiansManual.subtitle: Knowledge is Protection. Calm is Strength.
guardiansManual.homeCardDesc: Printable single-sheet crisis reference with legal scripts, reporting steps, and emergency checklist.
guardiansManual.stoicQuote: You have power over your mind — not outside events. Realize this, and you will find strength.
guardiansManual.stoicAcceptDesc: If an encounter happens, do not waste energy on "Why is this happening?" Focus entirely on "What is my legal duty right now?"
guardiansManual.stoicBreatheDesc: Panic leads to waived rights. Breathe. Speak slowly. Use the scripts exactly as written.
guardiansManual.stoicDutyDesc: You are not just protecting yourself; by exercising your rights, you are upholding the law for your entire neighborhood.
guardiansManual.scenarioATitle: Scenario A: A Knock at the Door
guardiansManual.scenarioARule: Do NOT open the door. Opening the door can be interpreted as "consent" to search.
guardiansManual.scenarioAScript: I do not consent to you entering my home. Please slide any judicial warrant signed by a judge or magistrate under the door. Otherwise, I have nothing to say to you.
guardiansManual.scenarioAWarrant: If they have a warrant: Check that it has your correct address and a signature. If it is an "Administrative Warrant" (Form I-200 or I-205), it does not give them the right to enter your home without consent.
guardiansManual.scenarioBTitle: Scenario B: Stopped in Public / In a Vehicle
guardiansManual.scenarioBRule: Keep your hands visible. Do not run.
guardiansManual.scenarioBScript1Note: If yes, walk away calmly. If no, proceed to the next line.
guardiansManual.scenarioBScript2: I am exercising my Fifth Amendment right to remain silent. I will not answer any questions regarding my birthplace, citizenship, or travel history. I want to speak to an attorney.
guardiansManual.mapIntro: If you witness enforcement activity, use safeneighbor.us to alert the network.
guardiansManual.mapObserveDesc: Note the number of agents, types of vehicles, and if they are wearing "POLICE" or "ICE/DHS" identifiers.
guardiansManual.mapPinDesc: Drop a pin on the map. Use the "Jitter" feature for your own privacy.
guardiansManual.mapVerifyDesc: If you see an existing pin, "Verify" it so neighbors know the information is current.
guardiansManual.checklistPhoneDesc: Ensure your device is ready to access scripts or document.
guardiansManual.checklistContactDesc: Have a family member's number memorized.
guardiansManual.checklistBookmarkDesc: Have the app icon on your phone's home screen.
guardiansManual.checklistSilenceDesc: Remember, you cannot "talk your way out" of an encounter. Only a lawyer can speak for you.
guardiansManual.footerTagline: Privacy-focused defaults. Minimal data. Practical protection.
guardiansManual.footerDisclaimer: This document is for educational purposes only and does not constitute legal advice. Consult a licensed attorney for specific legal situations.
